title: Squirrels, Ahoy!
summary: Josh and Chuck explore squirrels: about 300 species grouped into ground squirrels, tree squirrels, and flying squirrels. Topics include the Sciurus name pronunciation, prairie dog towns, tree squirrel dreys and communal winter huddles, scent-trail seed caching and forest planting, flying squirrel gliding, squirrel migrations and historic stampedes, the near-extinction of squirrels in 19th-century America and their reintroduction to urban parks (Olmsted, Central Park), attitudes toward squirrels as vermin and invasive species, feeding squirrels safely, road-crossing behavior, and black squirrels of New York. The episode ends with listener mail from a Baltimore kindergarten class about the Three Sisters.

segments.title: Opening listener anecdote
segments.summary: Josh opens with a personal story about his daughter Momo changing his view of squirrels, then the show intro plays.

segments.title: Banter and squirrel pronunciation
segments.summary: Hosts banter about squirrels, debate how to pronounce the family name Sciuridae, note there are about 300 species living on nearly every continent except Antarctica, and describe the bushy tail and jaw-muscle features that define squirrels. They also mention Atlanta's abundant squirrels and a close encounter with a squirrel.

segments.title: Ground squirrels overview
segments.summary: Josh introduces three groupings: ground, tree, and flying squirrels. Ground squirrels include chipmunks, groundhogs, prairie dogs, and marmots, which generally stay on the ground and are more communal.

segments.title: Prairie dog towns and ground squirrel communication
segments.summary: The largest recorded prairie dog town, a black-tailed prairie dog colony in Texas, is described as enormous. Ground squirrels have strong scent recognition of relatives and sophisticated alarm calls for predators, and sitting up on hind legs is noted.

segments.title: Tree squirrels and dreys
segments.summary: Tree squirrels, such as the Eastern gray, live in trees. Their nests, called dreys, are visible as stick masses in winter. Tree squirrels huddle communally in dreys for warmth in cold weather.

segments.title: Squirrel anatomy and behavior on trees
segments.summary: Hosts describe a winter nest scene, the ability of tree squirrels to rotate their hind feet to descend trees headfirst, and the startling effect this has on people. Chasing between squirrels is discussed as part of mating behavior.

segments.title: Scent glands and seed caching
segments.summary: Squirrels have scent glands in various locations depending on species; tree squirrels have them on their feet and use scent trails to find buried food. Their forgotten caches help plant trees, making them forest gardeners. Squirrels also fake burying nuts when another squirrel is watching. Ground squirrels use scent to mark territory, and some rub rattlesnake skin on themselves for camouflage.

segments.title: Flying squirrels and gliding
segments.summary: Hosts discuss flying squirrels, which are nocturnal and therefore seldom seen. They glide rather than fly, using a skin membrane (patagium) between their legs and steering with their tails, covering up to about 150 feet. Comparisons to wingsuits follow.

segments.title: Endangered flying squirrels and wildlife land bridges
segments.summary: Carolina northern flying squirrels are endangered. Hosts discuss wildlife crossings over highways, including the Robert Evans Memorial Animal Land Bridge in Los Angeles, and radio-tagged squirrels that crossed successfully.

segments.title: American chestnut forests and squirrel diet
segments.summary: Squirrel populations historically correlated with mast-producing trees such as chestnut, beech, and oak; a saying claimed squirrels could travel from Maine to Georgia without touching ground. Squirrels are opportunistic omnivores, have constantly growing incisors that need wearing down by cracking nuts, red squirrels in Maine tap sugar maples, and squirrels learn by observing one another.

segments.title: Squirrels in Australia
segments.summary: Squirrels were introduced to Australia in the nineteenth century, including the Eastern gray and the Indian palm squirrel in Perth. Those introduced populations died out, though feral colonies from zoo escapes in Perth may persist.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Short break before the next segment.

segments.title: Squirrel migrations and persecution as vermin
segments.summary: Historic squirrel migrations involved thousands of squirrels moving together after bumper food years followed by poor ones. Squirrels crossed fields and rivers and were hunted, eaten, and sold for pelts by farmers who saw them as crop-raiding vermin. Squirrels were nearly gone from America by the mid-to-late nineteenth century.

segments.title: Urban parks and squirrel reintroduction
segments.summary: Squirrels were reintroduced to city parks in the 1840s and 1850s, and Frederick Law Olmsted's large urban park movement brought many squirrels back. Philadelphia and Boston are mentioned as early examples. The Boy Scouts co-founder Ernest Thompson Seton argued that squirrels could curb boys' cruelty.

segments.title: Hunting squirrels today
segments.summary: Hosts note that some people still hunt and eat squirrels, especially in parts of Appalachia, and that hunting squirrels with a small rifle is a family tradition for some.

segments.title: Invasive Eastern gray squirrels and Scottish red squirrels
segments.summary: Eastern gray squirrels are considered invasive in Italy and have displaced Eurasian red squirrels in Britain, with about three quarters of the red population now in Scotland. Hosts reference the Scottish Squirrels website and an RSPCA article on feeding and habitat.

segments.title: Feeding squirrels safely
segments.summary: Hosts advise planting appropriate trees and offering unshelled nuts, acorns, and chopped fruits and vegetables rather than black safflower seeds or salted or honey-roasted nuts; raw peanuts can carry aflatoxin. Feeding can make squirrels dependent and cause problems. Chuck describes a trail camera showing wildlife visits.

segments.title: Why squirrels run into the road
segments.summary: Squirrels freeze when they see predators and then dart sideways; this instinct misfires with cars, which move in a straight line. Advice: slow down and watch for squirrels.

segments.title: Black squirrels of New York
segments.summary: Black squirrels are a dark color variant of the Eastern gray, caused by a recessive gene. They are more common in dense populations such as Roosevelt Island in New York, and possibly were once more dominant. Chuck cites an Untapped Cities article by Michelle Young.

segments.title: Kindergarten listener mail on the Three Sisters
segments.summary: A Baltimore City kindergarten class writes about learning the Three Sisters (corn, beans, and squash) and shares facts about planting, soil, and drying. Hosts promise a future Three Sisters episode.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh gives the email contact, and the outro plays.
